quotes.text: Tuning isn't a configuration event, it's a measurement loop. You set a policy, you measure what it catches and what it misses. You adjust and you do it again.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: States the episode's core thesis as a reusable principle.

quotes.text: The system doesn't merge policies. It doesn't take the stricter setting from each one it finds the first match, applies that policy and ignores everything below it.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Explains the policy precedence behaviour that silently overrides custom policies.

quotes.text: The old detection question was, is this message bad? That question fails here because the message isn't bad. It's clean. The new question is, is this message who it claims to be?
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Captures why impersonation attacks need identity-based detection.

quotes.text: A tenant where fewer people click and more people report has built something real. A tenant where fewer people click and almost nobody reports has just taught people to ignore mail they don't trust.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Shows why report rate matters more than click rate in phishing simulations.

quotes.text: The policy that protects you isn't the one you shipped, it's the one you reviewed last quarter. That's the difference between a tenant with controls and a tenant with protection.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: A memorable closing line on continuous review.

chapters.title: Why defaults fail: tuning as a measurement loop
Plan 1 versus Plan 2 and what you are licensed for
Preset security policies and policy precedence
SPF, DKIM, DMARC and phishing thresholds
Safe Links, Safe Attachments and exception debt
Attack simulation, metrics and the operating rhythm

takeaways: Start with the standard and strict preset policies, check which policy actually applies to each user because the first match wins, and keep custom policies only for documented, owned exceptions.

Impersonation protection, Safe Links and Safe Attachments only work as well as the protected lists, DMARC enforcement and do-not-rewrite exceptions behind them, so every exception needs an owner, a reason and an expiry date.

Measure delivered phish, report rate, time to remediate and false positives on a monthly and quarterly rhythm, and use attack simulation and Threat Explorer to tune instead of setting policies once and forgetting them.
hook: Most tenants run Microsoft Defender for Office 365 on defaults and assume they are protected while attackers test their filters every day. This episode is for email security admins, security engineers and SOC teams who want to tune anti-phishing, Safe Links, Safe Attachments and quarantine into a measurable loop that reduces both missed threats and false positives.
